summary: This document gives an implementation-independent basis for handling Aggregated Flows in IPFIX, which are flows representing packets from multiple original flows with common properties. It does so with detailed terminology and a description of an Intermediate Aggregation Process architecture, including methods for counting and distributing counters.

eli5.summary: Many small traffic records can be merged into bigger summary ones. This explains how to do that and keep the counts right.

questions: what is an intermediate aggregation process
subtitle: How to merge many IPFIX flows into fewer summary flows without losing track of the counts.

tldr.problem: Network operators often need to combine many flow records into fewer ones, for traffic matrices, time series or long-term storage, but there was no common description of how to do this interoperably.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 7015 defines Aggregated Flows and an Intermediate Aggregation Process built from four operations: interval distribution, key aggregation, value aggregation and aggregate combination. It adds Information Elements for flow counts, distinct host counts and the method used to spread counters across intervals.
tldr.outcome: Aggregated data can be exported with the unchanged IPFIX protocol, and a receiver can tell how the counters were distributed. It is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted.

today: RFC 7015 is a Proposed Standard published in September 2013, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on RFC 7011, and RFC 7014 is the related document on selecting flows.

sections.title: Why Aggregate Flows
sections.content:
Aggregating flows into records that stand for several flows is a common way to analyse and reduce data. The RFC lists traffic matrix calculation, time series for visualisation or anomaly detection, and data reduction for long-term trending and storage. Depending on the keys, it can also have an anonymizing effect, for example when IP addresses are removed.

An Aggregated Flow is still a Flow, so the IPFIX protocol (RFC 7011) can export it and the IPFIX File Format can store it as is. No protocol changes are needed. The RFC instead supplies a common terminology, an architecture for the Intermediate Aggregation Process (IAP) and methods for counting Original Flows and distributing counters across intervals. Sections 5, 6 and 7 are normative.
sections.eli5: Instead of keeping a note for every little thing, you keep one bigger note that sums them up. It saves space and is easier to read.

sections.title: Key Terms
sections.content:
An Original Flow is a Flow given as input to an IAP. An Aggregated Flow is a Flow derived from a set of zero or more Original Flows within a defined Aggregation Interval, a time interval imposed on it. An Original Flow that is partially or completely represented in an Aggregated Flow is a Contributing Flow.

A Partially Aggregated Flow is the intermediate data structure inside the IAP while aggregation is in progress. The Original Exporter is the Exporter that sent the Original Flows, which matters only when the IAP runs on a Mediator. The RFC says these definitions refine, and do not contradict, the terms in the earlier Mediation documents.
sections.eli5: The original small records are the ingredients, and the combined record is the finished dish. The kitchen that does the mixing is the Intermediate Aggregation Process.

sections.title: Where Aggregation Happens and How It Is Built
sections.content:
An IAP can sit in three places: in the Metering Process at an Exporter, in a Mediator between an Exporter and a Collector, or at a Collector, where it can pass Aggregated Flows to a File Writer for storage. Mediators are the most flexible arrangement and are the usual place, and an IAP can also take already Aggregated Flows from an upstream IAP.

Inside the IAP the RFC models four operations on Partially Aggregated Flows. Interval distribution is temporal and imposes the Aggregation Interval. Key aggregation and value aggregation are spatial and change the Flow Key fields or the non-key fields. Aggregate combination merges flows that share Flow Key values and interval into one Aggregated Flow. The first three may run any number of times in any order, but since any spatial operation implies a temporal one, at least one interval distribution step, even implicit, is required.

An optional correlation and normalization step handles Original Flows from several Metering Processes that give different views of the same flow, merging them as if measured by one process that used the union of all their fields. Its exact steps are left to implementations. Because aggregate combination is idempotent, several IAPs in series can be modelled as one.
sections.eli5: It is like an assembly line with four stations: sort by time, simplify the labels, add up the numbers, and pack everything that matches into one box.

sections.title: Interval Distribution
sections.content:
The interval can be regular, such as every five minutes, irregular, or derived from the Original Flows themselves. Shorter intervals give higher resolution and faster reaction. Longer intervals give more data reduction and simpler counter distribution. If the interval is longer than the longest Original Flow, a flow can cross at most one boundary and contribute to at most two Aggregated Flows. A common choice then is to account it all to the first or to the last interval.

When the interval is shorter than some Original Flows, the IAP must spread the counters. The RFC lists methods from simple to accurate: Start Interval, End Interval, Mid Interval, Simple Uniform Distribution, Proportional Uniform Distribution, Simulated Process and Direct. Counters MUST be distributed so that the total count is preserved, within the limits of accuracy of the implementation, and all counters in a given Aggregated Flow MUST use the same method.

Flows may arrive in any order, so the IAP buffers Partially Aggregated Flows in current intervals. It SHOULD accept start and end times in any reasonable order, and interval expiry MUST be configurable where reasonable order is not obvious. Time Composition is a special case that joins matching flows split by a short active timeout into one longer flow. Alternatively, Original Exporters can be configured to align their flow times with the desired interval.
sections.eli5: If a long phone call crosses midnight, you must decide which day it counts for, or split it between the two days. Different methods answer that in different ways.

sections.title: Key and Value Aggregation
sections.content:
Key aggregation builds new Flow Keys for the Aggregated Flows in two ways. Reduction drops fields or precision, for example removing ports, protocol and type of service, keeping the source address and masking the destination address to a /24 network. Replacement swaps fields for derived ones, for example looking up an AS number for each address. A field can also be promoted to a key, as when grouping flows by packet count.

Key aggregation can add counters. Original Flows can be counted in two ways. Conservative counting gives each Original Flow exactly one in total, so the sum over all Aggregated Flows equals the number of Original Flows. Non-conservative counting counts every Aggregated Flow an Original Flow appears in, so the sum is greater than or equal to the number of Original Flows. In the RFC's example of three flows A, B and C under Start Interval distribution, the conservative counts are 3, 0 and 0, while the non-conservative counts are 3, 2 and 1.

Distinct key values removed during aggregation can be counted, such as distinct sources per destination. Value aggregation can add other statistics, and the RFC mentions sample entropy as a useful anomaly-detection signal: one host scanning many others lowers source address entropy and raises target address entropy. When flows are finally combined, delta counters are summed and flags are unioned. Approximate counting, such as Bloom filters, is allowed where exactness matters less.
sections.eli5: Reducing a key is like writing only the street and not the house number. Counting the flows is like counting how many letters went into each mailbag.

sections.title: Exporting Aggregated Flows
sections.content:
Aggregated Flows are exported like any other Flow. Existing timestamp elements such as flowStartMilliseconds already carry the interval, so each Aggregated Flow with timing information SHOULD contain both an interval start and an interval end.

New Information Elements cover the counts: originalFlowsPresent (375, non-conservative), originalFlowsInitiated (376, conservative, first packet in this flow), originalFlowsCompleted (377, conservative, last packet in this flow) and deltaFlowCount (3, conservative, distributable by any method). Six elements, IDs 378 to 383, hold distinct counts of source and destination addresses, with preference for the version-independent ones unless the IP version matters.

An Exporting Process MAY send an Aggregate Counter Distribution Option Record for a Template. It is an Options Template with the Template ID as scope and the valueDistributionMethod element (ID 384). When no record is available, a Collecting Process should assume Start Interval. The record is only needed in unusual cases such as intervals shorter than the Original Flows.
sections.eli5: When you send the summary, you attach a small note saying how you split up the numbers, so the reader knows how to interpret them.

sections.title: Delay, Sampling and Mixed Inputs
sections.content:
The IAP must wait for all Original Flows that might belong to an interval. This is dominated by the Metering Process active timeout. With a five-minute active timeout the IAP adds a delay of at least five minutes, and with several Metering Processes the maximum active timeout sets the delay. If a flow arrives after its interval closed, the IAP MAY drop it.

The effect of sampling on aggregation is described as still an open research question. To keep results comparable, the RFC advises aggregating only flows sampled with the same rate and algorithm, or flows normalized to look that way. For mixed Flow types, aggregate separately and use the Observation Domain ID to tell outputs apart, or correlate flows first if the same packet may be seen at two Observation Points.
sections.eli5: You cannot add up the day's sales until the last customer has been counted, so there is always a wait. And you should only combine counts that were taken the same way.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
RFC 7015 adds no new protocol, so the security considerations in Section 11 of RFC 7011 apply. When aggregation runs on a Mediator, the Mediator considerations in Section 9 of RFC 6183 apply as well.

Aggregation that removes identifiers can have an anonymizing effect and may be combined with anonymization in a Mediator. If it is used as part of a data protection scheme, the considerations in Section 9 of RFC 6235 also apply.
sections.eli5: Combining records can hide who did what, but it is not magic. If privacy matters, follow the extra privacy rules too.

viz.caption: OPERATIONS INSIDE AN INTERMEDIATE AGGREGATION PROCESS

items.title: Key aggregation
items.text: Spatial. Adds, changes or removes Flow Key fields.

items.title: Value aggregation
items.text: Spatial. Adds, changes or removes non-key fields.

items.title: Aggregate combination
items.text: Merges flows sharing keys and interval into one Aggregated Flow.

items.title: Correlation and normalization
items.text: Optional. Unifies different views of the same flow first.

items.label: Unspecified
items.desc: Counters explicitly not distributed by any other defined method.

items.label: Start Interval
items.desc: Counters go to the interval containing the flow start. Assumed default if unknown.

items.label: End Interval
items.desc: Counters go to the interval containing the flow end.

items.label: Mid Interval
items.desc: Counters go to a single interval containing a time between start and end.

items.label: Simple Uniform Distribution
items.desc: Counters divided by the number of intervals covered.

items.label: Proportional Uniform Distribution
items.desc: Mean rate times the time overlapping each interval.

items.label: Simulated Process
items.desc: Distributed by a function based on flows presumed to be similar.
